title: Walls of Earth
description: Mud brick, cob and rammed earth, the first mud-brick towns, and why earth walls feel steady
tryIt: Do a jar test: shake a handful of garden soil in a jar of water, leave it for a few days, and watch it settle into layers from coarse at the bottom to fine on top.

concepts.title: How it works: walls of earth
concepts.contentHtml:
It is spring of your first year. The debris hut got you through the winter, but it leaks, it sags and the mice have moved in. You want proper walls. You look down at your boots, caked in sticky mud, and realise that the oldest building material on Earth is the one you are standing on.

People have built with earth for at least 11,000 years. Jericho is one of the earliest settlements known, dated back to 9000 BCE, and there the first villagers lived in round houses about 5 metres across, built with clay and straw. A later settlement there had rectangular buildings made of mudbricks. At Çatalhöyük in Turkey, first settled around 7400 BCE, houses were packed so tightly that there were no streets at all: people walked across the roofs and climbed down a wooden ladder through a hole in the ceiling. The walls were mud brick, and at its peak somewhere between 3,500 and 8,000 people lived there.

Three methods have lasted ever since:

  • Adobe: sand, clay, water and often straw or grass, pressed into wooden moulds and dried by the sun, never fired in a kiln.
  • Cob: a stiff, lumpy mix of clay, marl or chalk with gravel and straw, piled up wet in courses called lifts.
  • Rammed earth: damp soil compacted in layers inside formwork, making thick, freestanding walls of about 2,000 kilograms per cubic metre.

Clay is the glue in all three. Its tiny particles coat the sand and gravel and bind them as the mix dries, and the result is heavy, cheap and close at hand: the cob builders of the New Forest usually dug their clay or chalk from the ground close to the building.

concepts.title: In the field: raising a cob wall
concepts.contentHtml:
You cannot test a wall by waiting a century, so borrow the experience of people who did. Builders in Devon summed it up in one line: give a cob wall a good hat and a good pair of boots, and it will stand for a very long time. Here is how a traditional cob wall goes up, from the ground to the roof.

  1. Read your soil. Drop a little into a jar of water, shake it and leave it for a few days. It settles into layers that show roughly what your soil is made of.
  2. Dig close to home. Earth is heavy, so traditional builders dug it beside the site.
  3. Put on the boots. Start with a plinth of stone or brick that lifts the earth clear of the wet ground. It is denser than cob and cuts the moisture drawn up into the wall.
  4. Mix in the straw. Work straw through the wet clay to bind it.
  5. Build in lifts. Pile the wet mix up in layers; on walls with no render you can still see them as bands.
  6. Put on the hat. Give the roof an overhang of 400 to 700 mm, enough to throw rain clear of the wall and stop it splashing and eroding the foot.
  7. Finish with lime, never cement. Lime render or limewash lets the wall dry out. Rigid cement render cracks, traps water behind it, and in winter the water freezes and bursts the render off.
Safety Earth walls are heavy, and soaked earth loses its strength: the New Forest guidance warns that a constant build-up of water can cause an instant and dramatic slump in which whole sections of wall fail. Never dig into the foot of an old earth wall, never shelter beside one that is wet through or bulging, and lift with your legs, not your back. Anything people will sleep under should be checked by someone qualified, and may need permission where you live.

concepts.title: Myth check: straw, mud and warmth
concepts.contentHtml:
Earth buildings attract folklore. Two beliefs come up again and again, and both are half right.

Myth Straw reinforces mud bricks, like steel bars in concrete.
Reality The US National Park Service's guide to adobe says straw and grass do not reinforce the bricks or give them long-term strength. What they do is help the bricks shrink more evenly as they dry, so fewer of them crack. The real strength comes from the balance of clay and sand in the soil.
Myth Thick earth walls are wonderful insulation.
Reality They are wonderful at storing heat, which is a different thing. A thick rammed-earth wall slows heat down, so on a summer day the inside stays cooler and the indoor peak arrives several hours after the outdoor one. That delay is what makes many people think the walls insulate well. A laboratory test by Australia's CSIRO in 2000 measured the thermal resistance of rammed earth at 0.4 square metre kelvins per watt: about the same as a brick wall, and far worse than any insulating material. In winter, an unheated mud-brick house could fall to about 12 °C inside when it was 3 °C outside.

Wait, really? The steadiness is real, and thickness buys time. In one study's calculations, the delay through a rammed-earth wall grew from about 2.8 hours at 110 mm thick to 6.2 hours at 220 mm and 9.3 hours at 330 mm. In a hot, dry climate that is exactly what you want: the afternoon heat is still working its way through the wall when the cool of the night arrives. In a cold one you also need a fire, or insulation, or both.

title: Burning Stone: Lime
description: Turning limestone into quicklime, slaking it, and why lime mortar turns back into stone
tryIt: Look closely at an old brick wall: check whether the mortar is softer than the bricks, and whether bricks next to hard, grey patches of repair have cracked or flaked.

concepts.title: How it works: the lime cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
The autumn rains are eating your new mud walls. To protect them, and to glue stones together, you need something that sets hard and stays hard in the wet. Your ancestors found it by doing something that sounds mad: they set fire to rocks.

Burn limestone, chalk, marble or even seashells above 900 °C and the heat drives off carbon dioxide, leaving quicklime (calcium oxide). The Roman architect Vitruvius noticed that the stone came out of the kiln the same size it went in, but about a third lighter. Put quicklime in water and it reacts violently: up to the mid-19th century builders slaked lump lime on site, and the mixing made it boil. What is left is slaked lime (calcium hydroxide), a creamy putty that was left to mature in a pit for several weeks, up to a year.

Now the clever bit. Mix the putty with sand, about one part to three, and lay it between stones. Over the following weeks it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and turns back into calcium carbonate, the same chemical as the rock you started with. Builders call this carbonation, and the whole loop is the lime cycle.

It is ancient. The Building Limes Forum dates the earliest surviving lime binder to around 8000 BC, in a floor in Turkey, and the second settlement at Jericho had terrazzo floors made of lime. Limes were the principal binders of the Roman Empire, and of castles, cathedrals, bridges and harbours, until cement pushed them aside in the 19th century.

concepts.title: In the field: from rock to mortar
concepts.contentHtml:
For thousands of years every district that built in stone had its lime kilns: stone pots in which limestone was cooked until it fell apart. Here is how lime was made and used, step by step. Read it as history, not as a project: the safety card explains why.

  1. Choose pure stone. Vitruvius and Pliny specified pure white limestone, free of impurities.
  2. Burn it. Hold the stone above 900 °C until the carbon dioxide is gone. There is no short cut: Vitruvius notes that raw limestone pounded small and mixed with sand never sets.
  3. Slake it. Add the quicklime to water and stand well back as it heats and boils.
  4. Let it mature. Keep the putty wet in a pit or box for weeks or months.
  5. Mix the mortar. About one part putty to three parts sand by volume.
  6. Let it set slowly. Shade fresh lime work from sun and wind: lime mortar that dries too fast carbonates less and stays weak.
Safety Do not burn or slake lime yourself. Quicklime is corrosive to the eyes, skin and lungs, and the international chemical safety card warns of severe deep burns to the eyes. Its reaction with water can give off enough heat to ignite combustible materials nearby. Slaked lime and fresh lime mortar are caustic too. If you ever use any lime product, wear safety goggles, gloves and long sleeves, and keep the dust out of your lungs. Lime in the eye is an emergency: rinse with plenty of clean water for several minutes and get medical help straight away.

concepts.title: Myth check: hard is not better
concepts.contentHtml:
Lime fell out of fashion in the 20th century, and a pair of myths grew up in its place.

Myth Mortar sets by drying out, like mud.
Reality Lime mortar hardens by a chemical reaction with the air: it takes in carbon dioxide and turns back into stone. Dry it too quickly and less of it carbonates, so it ends up weaker. Hydraulic limes, burnt from stone with impurities such as aluminium and magnesium silicates, also set chemically and can harden under water.
Myth The harder the mortar, the stronger the wall.
Reality The US National Park Service calls it a common error to assume that hardness or high strength is a measure of appropriateness. Walls move as they heat, cool, get wet and settle. Soft mortar takes up the movement and cracks along the joints, which is easy to repoint. Mortar harder than the bricks will not give, so the bricks crack and spall instead, damage that cannot be repaired easily. Evidence of the harm done by cement mortars emerged in the 1970s and started a revival of lime.

Wait, really? Lime can mend itself. When a lime wall moves it tends to form many fine cracks rather than one big one. Rain dissolves a little of the free lime and carries it into the cracks; as the water evaporates, the lime is left behind and begins to seal them. Builders call this autogenous, or self-healing. The Romans, as you will see in lesson four, may have pushed the same trick much further.

title: Timber, Joints and Trusses
description: Neolithic carpenters, mortise and tenon joints, why trusses are triangles, and green wood
tryIt: Make a square and a triangle from lolly sticks or card strips joined with drawing pins, push sideways on a corner of each, and feel which one holds its shape.

concepts.title: How it works: the first carpenters
concepts.contentHtml:
Earth and lime make walls, but a roof has to span a gap, and for that you need timber and a way to join it without a single nail. Look around the woods: everything you need is standing there.

The oldest proof that people could do this comes from the bottom of wells. In eastern Germany archaeologists excavated four Early Neolithic wells lined with oak, which survived for thousands of years below the water table while the timber houses of the same farmers left only marks in the soil. Tree rings date them to the year: one well was built from 13 oaks felled in 5102 BC.

Those first farmers felled oaks up to 300 years old and a metre across using stone adzes. They split the logs with wooden wedges driven by wooden mauls, cut timbers to length partly by burning, and smoothed them with adzes. Two wells stood on base frames made with mortise and tenon joints, and in one the tenons poked through and were locked with wooden wedges. The team concluded that the first farmers were also the first carpenters, and that their work overturns the old belief that metal was needed for complex timber building.

A mortise is a slot; a tenon is a tongue cut on the end of another timber to fit it. Push them together, drive a peg or wedge through both, and two timbers are locked at a right angle with no metal at all. Seven thousand years later, carpenters still use exactly the same idea.

concepts.title: In the field: frames and roofs
concepts.contentHtml:
Once you can join two timbers, you can join many. The next problem is the roof: its weight pushes the tops of the walls outwards. The answer, worked out by carpenters long before anyone wrote it down, is the triangle.

A square frame with pinned corners can fold into a lozenge without any timber changing length. A triangle cannot: three fixed sides allow only one shape. In a king post truss the two sloping rafters resist compression, while the tie beam along the bottom acts in tension, holding the rafters' feet together so the load goes down into the walls instead of shoving them apart. The central king post also works in tension. The Venetian architect Andrea Palladio is usually credited with the first published description of a truss.

  1. Fell in one go. Medieval roofs and frames were often cut from trees all felled in a single campaign, then put up within a short time.
  2. Split and hew. Split logs along the grain with wedges, then dress the faces flat.
  3. Cut joints while green. Fresh wood is far easier to work than seasoned.
  4. Peg, do not nail. A tight wooden peg through mortise and tenon holds the frame.
  5. Triangulate. Brace rectangles with diagonals and tie the feet of every pair of rafters.
  6. Keep it dry. Rot needs liquid water in the wood, which for most species means above about 24 to 32 percent moisture.
Safety Felling and hewing cause serious injuries. Never fell a tree without training and the landowner's permission, keep well clear of the line of fall, and never stand under a timber being lifted or rolled. Big timbers are far heavier than they look: move them with several people, levers and rollers, and keep hands and feet out from underneath. Keep axe and adze edges sharp and covered when not in use.

concepts.title: Myth check: seasoning and covered bridges
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Good medieval carpenters seasoned their oak for years before building with it.
Reality Mostly they did not. Tree-ring specialists say most medieval woodworkers used green wood, because seasoned wood is much more difficult to work, so the felling date of a building's timbers usually gives the year it went up. Big projects were the exception: for cathedral roofs and large monastic buildings, trees were more often felled over a number of seasons and the timbers stockpiled for a few years.

Building green has a price, and the old carpenters knew it. The US covered bridge manual defines seasoned wood as below 19 percent moisture and green wood as above it. Green wood shrinks after it is built in, while seasoned timber hardly changes size. It also shrinks by different amounts around the growth rings and across them, which is why a beam with the heart boxed in its middle is much more prone to twisting and splitting as it dries.

Myth Covered bridges were roofed to shelter travellers.
Reality The manual admits many popular explanations, then gives the simplest and most common reason: to protect the timber. The first uncovered timber bridges failed in just a few years from rot, because chemical preservatives were not available or used. North American covered bridges still serve after nearly 200 years, thanks partly to the trusses staying sound under their roofs.

Wait, really? The roof was cheap insurance. Builders reckoned that maintaining and now and then replacing the light covering was far easier than building a whole new bridge.

title: Stone, Arches and the Pantheon
description: Compression and tension, how arches stand, raising one on centring, and Roman concrete
tryIt: Hang a light chain or necklace between your hands, photograph it, then turn the photo upside down: you are looking at the shape of a strong arch.

concepts.title: How it works: squeeze, never stretch
concepts.contentHtml:
Your timber roof is up, but you want a doorway through a stone wall, a bridge over the stream, a cellar that will outlast you. Stone is the strongest thing around, as long as you only ever squeeze it. Stretch it and it snaps: engineers who analyse old arches simply assume that masonry has no tensile strength at all.

That is the trouble with a stone beam, or lintel. Lay one across a gap and load it, and the top is squeezed while the bottom is stretched, so the bottom cracks first. Galileo found that the breaking force on a beam increases as the square of its length, one reason stone lintels stay short.

The arch turns every load into a squeeze. Its wedge-shaped stones, the voussoirs, have joints radiating to the centre, as Vitruvius described them. Under load they press on each other and down into the supports, but they also push outwards, so Vitruvius warned that the end piers must be built broader than the rest, to resist the wedges pressing along their joints and thrusting out the abutments.

What is the best shape? Robert Hooke announced to the Royal Society around 1671 that he knew, but published it in 1675 only as a scrambled anagram. His executor decoded it in 1705: as hangs a flexible cable, so inverted, stand the touching pieces of an arch. A hanging chain is pure tension; flip its curve and you get pure compression. A century later Coulomb gave the rule engineers still use: an arch is stable as long as its line of thrust, the path the forces take, lies within the masonry.

concepts.title: In the field: raising an arch
concepts.contentHtml:
An arch has an awkward secret: it cannot hold itself up until it is finished. Half an arch is just a heap of stones waiting to fall. So builders cheat with a temporary wooden frame, and the order of work is everything.

  1. Build the abutments first, and big. They must take the arch's sideways push as well as its weight.
  2. Make a centring. A timber frame cut to the curve of the underside of the arch, propped firmly from the ground.
  3. Cut the voussoirs. Every stone is a wedge, its joints pointing to the centre of the curve.
  4. Lay from both sides at once. Work up from each abutment so the centring is loaded evenly.
  5. Drop in the keystone. The last stone, at the crown, closes the ring. Only now is it an arch.
  6. Strike the centring. Ease the frame down and out. The arch settles a little and fine cracks open between stones; as one engineering paper puts it, masonry arches crack inexorably after decentering, something well known to any master builder.

Watch where the thrust goes. In a row of arches, each one's sideways push is balanced by its neighbour's, and only the end arches push against nothing but their abutments. That is why Vitruvius wanted the outermost piers built broader than the rest, and why a bridge that loses one arch puts its neighbours at risk.

Safety Stone is heavy and arches fail suddenly. Never stand under an arch while its centring is being struck, never knock out a prop you did not put in, and never climb on or under ruined arches, walls or bridges: one missing stone can leave the thrust with nowhere to go. Wear stout boots and gloves when moving stone, and get help with anything you cannot lift easily.

concepts.title: Myth check: keystones and Roman concrete
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The keystone holds the whole arch up.
Reality It is simply the last voussoir in. What keeps an arch standing is geometry: if the line of thrust touches the edge of the masonry, a hinge forms between two stones, and enough hinges let the arch fold. So a cracked arch is not necessarily doomed. A corollary of the safe theorem says that if a line of thrust can be drawn within the arch, it will not collapse, and engineers now regard cracking as irrelevant to safety.
Myth Roman concrete was a lost secret.
Reality It was clever chemistry, now being worked out. The Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash; Vitruvius wrote that a powder from around Vesuvius, mixed with lime and rubble, would set hard even under the sea. In 2023 an MIT team argued that the white lumps of lime in Roman concrete, long dismissed as sloppy mixing, came from mixing in hot quicklime and let cracks heal: in their tests, cracks in hot-mixed concrete sealed within two weeks, while the same mix without quicklime never healed.

Wait, really? The Pantheon in Rome, dedicated in 128 CE, still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome. Its rotunda is 43.2 metres across and exactly as high, so a perfect sphere would fit inside. The dome is cast from a light mix of tufa and scoria, lightened further by rings of coffers, and open at the crown through an oculus 8.8 metres wide. Think of it as an arch spun round on its axis.

title: A Good Hat and Boots
description: Damp, foundations, roof pitch and thatch, and the myths about keeping a building dry
tryIt: On the next rainy day, walk round your home or an old building nearby and watch where the water goes: off the eaves, down the pipes, and how far from the wall it lands.

concepts.title: How it works: water is the enemy
concepts.contentHtml:
Your walls are up, your roof is on, and the first autumn gale hits. Now you learn what every builder learns: the real enemy is not wind or cold but water. The US National Park Service calls uncontrolled moisture the most prevalent cause of deterioration in older and historic buildings.

Water attacks from three directions. It falls from above, so the roof must shed it fast. It splashes up at the foot of the wall. And it creeps up from below by capillary action, the pull that draws water up a paper towel; in damp masonry this rising damp often leaves a whitish tide mark about 1 to 3 feet above the ground, where the water evaporates.

The roof is your first defence, and its pitch, or steepness, matters. The East Anglian master thatchers put it plainly: the steeper the thatch, the longer it lasts, because a steep roof sheds rain faster and its surface dries sooner, slowing fungal decay. They aim for at least 50 degrees.

Thatch grew from whatever was local. Straw, as long straw or combed wheat reed, was England's main thatch until the 19th century, and water reed was used in East Anglia and other wetlands. West Country roofs of combed wheat reed are shallow and rounded, compared with the steeply pitched long straw roofs of East Anglia. Then commercial Welsh slate production began in 1820, and canals and railways carried other materials far and wide.

concepts.title: In the field: keeping a house dry
concepts.contentHtml:
The old builders had no damp-proof membranes or plastic pipes, yet many of their houses have stayed dry for centuries. Their methods are worth copying, and none of them is complicated: keep water off, send it away, and let the walls dry out.

  1. Pick dry ground. Build where water drains away, never in a hollow.
  2. Slope the ground away. Shape the earth so rain runs away from the foundations, not towards them.
  3. Lead roof water away. Carry downpipe water well clear of the building, and stop it splashing back onto the foot of the wall.
  4. Wear boots. Stand earth and timber on a plinth of stone or brick. Where the water table is high, builders added a horizontal barrier such as a course of slate or a sheet of lead to stop moisture rising.
  5. Wear a hat. Deep eaves throw the drips clear of the wall.
  6. Go steep on top. For thatch, 50 degrees or more.
  7. Keep up the maintenance. Clear blocked gutters and downpipes, and on a thatched roof replace the ridge every 15 to 25 years.
Safety Much of this work happens at height. Never climb onto an old roof, a thatch or a ruin, never use a ladder without someone footing it, and keep ladders well away from overhead power lines. Do not dig beside or under foundations without expert advice. Thatch and open fires need respect: keep chimneys swept and sound, and keep bonfires and fireworks well away from a thatched roof.

concepts.title: Myth check: thatch, damp and fire
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Thatch soaks up rain like a sponge.
Reality The East Anglian master thatchers call this a common myth, and say it is not true for around 95% of UK thatch. On a well-made roof only the top 2 to 3 cm shows noticeable decay, and the thatch beneath stays bone dry and keeps its original colour. The surface wears down slowly, sometimes over two or three generations, until the fixings come near the top and it is time to rethatch. Many water reed roofs are known to have lasted at least 70 years.
Myth To cure a damp wall, seal it.
Reality The National Park Service warns against sealing damp into a wall with a waterproof coating such as cement or vinyl on the inside: it only forces the capillary damp, and its damage, higher up the wall. In one case an owner tested his theory about a wet basement by running roof water away through long pipes, and found he needed better drainage, not expensive waterproofing.

Wait, really? Thatch is not the fire trap people imagine, either. A 1995 conservation article quoted Dorset Fire Brigade figures: of 3,000 fires a year, only 8 to 10 involved thatched buildings, and in most of those the fire had started inside the building.
